analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate drug prices, taxes price spikes above inflation, and eases importing cheaper drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2021 and never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the government to negotiate prices for prescription drugs covered by Medicare, with a fallback price set at what the Veterans Affairs system pays if talks fail. It would have imposed a tax on drug companies whose prices rise faster than inflation, required drugmakers to disclose their research, marketing, and pricing costs, allowed personal imports of lower-priced drugs from Canada, capped patient cost-sharing, and forced manufacturers to pay rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees. It never advanced past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially low-income enrollees, would pay less for prescriptions; people with employer or marketplace plans would face capped out-of-pocket drug costs; and consumers would be able to buy qualifying medicines from certified Canadian pharmacies. Taxpayers would also benefit from lower Medicare drug spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare enrollees and people with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Replaces Medicare's 'non-interference' rule with a requirement that the government negotiate prices for high-cost Medicare drugs; if negotiation fails, the price is set at the lesser of the price the Department of Veterans Affairs pays [S3]
Imposes an excise tax on prescription drug price increases above inflation, reaching 50-100% of the extra revenue from a spike unless the manufacturer justifies it with input-cost increases [S3]
Requires drug manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate, benchmarked to the Medicaid rebate amount, for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare drug plan enrollees [S3]

Requires HHS to issue regulations letting wholesale distributors, pharmacies, and individuals import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada, including insulin and peritoneal dialysis solution for personal use, with certification and testing safeguards [S3]
Requires annual public reports from drugmakers on research spending, marketing, executive pay, revenues, and net prices, with civil penalties of up to $200,000 per day for incomplete reports [S3]

Lessens prescription drug cost-sharing requirements under qualified health plans and group health plans, and limits the market exclusivity that trade agreements must provide for biological products [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the direct cost: negotiated Medicare prices, the price-spike excise tax, rebates on low-income enrollees' drugs, new transparency compliance, and the loss of the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer advertising [S3]. Some of that cost would come out of industry revenue rather than being passed to patients.

drawbacks.text: When negotiations fail, the bill sets the Medicare price at the VA procurement price, a hard government-set fallback; opponents of Medicare negotiation argue this kind of price control could reduce manufacturers' investment in developing new medicines [S3]

The price-spike excise tax applies to increases above inflation, even cumulative ones reaching back over five years, unless the company wins an exemption, which manufacturers argued could penalize legitimate cost increases [S3]

Importation adds a new supply channel that the bill tries to make safe through certified sellers, laboratory testing, recall requirements, and prison terms of up to 10 years for fraudulent online pharmacies, but it still depends on foreign regulators and supply-chain checks working [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households that rely on prescription drugs, the benefits were substantial and concrete: lower Medicare prices, rebates for low-income enrollees, capped cost-sharing, and a legal route to cheaper Canadian drugs. The main honest trade-off is that pressuring brand-name drug revenue could slow investment in future medicines, and the government-set fallback price is an aggressive tool that could have been litigated and tested for years. The transparency and price-spike provisions were comparatively low-risk. On balance the bill's benefits to patients and taxpayers were large relative to its downsides, though its breadth made it a heavy lift politically.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tina Smith introduced the Affordable Medications Act on May 27, 2021, with 13 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S1][S3]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5]
No further action was ever recorded: no committee markup, no committee vote, and no Senate floor vote [S5]
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they kept their existing Medicare prices, faced no price-spike tax or new rebates, and avoided the transparency reporting the bill would have imposed. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The committee under his chairmanship never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it remained pending in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Opposed Medicare price negotiation and related government drug-pricing proposals during this period

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or independents (12 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents), with no Republican support, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill targets their revenue directly through Medicare price negotiation with a VA-price fallback, an excise tax on price spikes above inflation, rebates on drugs for low-income Medicare enrollees, and mandatory disclosure of R&D, marketing, and profits. Patients and taxpayers would have paid less because manufacturers would have received less.

The bill requires drugmakers to report the net prices realized by pharmacy benefit managers after rebates, shining light on the PBM rebate system but not restructuring it. The disclosure could pressure PBM practices without directly regulating them.

The bill directs the FDA to build a generic drug database, tightens the 180-day generic exclusivity rules to prevent gamesmanship, and bars 'pay for delay' compensation, all of which would speed cheaper generic competition to market.

The bill creates a certified-seller importation program letting licensed Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers sell qualifying drugs to U.S. importers and individuals, opening a new customer market while giving Americans a legal route to lower prices.

The bill adds new reporting requirements on how much assistance these programs provide for drugs made by their donors and orders a GAO study of whether manufacturer-funded copay coupons inflate drug prices. Programs face scrutiny but no funding cut.
